title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page of E740, presented to the St. Petersburg Academy on 8 March 1779 and printed posthumously in the Mémoires (dated 1813). It states the problem the paper addresses.

§1. Euler says that the existing theory of curves with a maximum or minimum property covers only plane curves. The reason is that the integral functional ∫Φ(x,y,y',…)dx involves just two variables. One seeks the relation y = y(x) that makes it extremal, and a curve so determined is given by one equation between two coordinates, so it lies in a plane.

§2 (finished on p.19). If the integrand involves three variables x, y, z, the integral has a definite value only when two of them are fixed as functions of the third, say y = y(x) and z = z(x). The extremum problem then asks for two relations at once. Read as coordinates, this is a space curve, given by two equations. These are, in effect, the equations of its projections on the planes AOB and AOC (Fig. 1).

In modern terms, the paper announces the calculus of variations for a functional J[y,z] = ∫F(x,y,z,y',z',…)dx with two unknown functions. That leads to a system of two Euler–Lagrange equations, ∂F/∂y − d/dx ∂F/∂y' + … = 0 and the same with z. Its intended applications are extremal space curves, such as shortest or isoperimetric curves in space and curves on surfaces.
errors: The historical claim in §1 overstates matters. Extremal problems for non-plane curves had already been treated. Geodesics on surfaces were handled by Johann Bernoulli and by Euler himself (E9, 1728/1732). Lagrange's δ-method of 1760–61 explicitly allowed several dependent functions. Euler's own later variational work, e.g. the 1760s papers on the method of variations, is also, as far as I know, general enough to cover several functions (unsure of details). As a rhetorical framing for 1779 the claim is understandable, but it is not literally true.
No mathematical errors on this page; it is purely introductory.

ideas.what: Extremal problems with two unknown functions y(x), z(x), interpreted as space curves given by two projection equations
ideas.modern_name: Calculus of variations for several dependent variables (systems of Euler–Lagrange equations); variational problems for curves in R^3
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–61, Misc. Taurinensia), with antecedents in geodesic problems (Joh. Bernoulli, Euler E9)
ideas.where_published: E9 (geodesics on surfaces); Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744) treats related extensions; E740 itself (Mém. Acad. St-Pétersbourg, 1813); Opera omnia I.25

ideas.what: Determining a space curve by two equations, x–y and x–z, i.e. by its projections on two coordinate planes
ideas.modern_name: Representation of a space curve as the intersection of two projecting cylinders
ideas.usually_credited_to: Clairaut (Recherches sur les courbes à double courbure, 1731); also Euler, Introductio Appendix (1748)
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vol. II, Appendix (E102)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an introductory page that restates a standard and already established extension of the calculus of variations to two dependent functions. Nothing on it is new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well. The running text in §1 reads 'Maximi Minimive'; the title reads 'MAXIMI VEL MINIMI'. Both are rendered correctly.
Next page, not this one: 'ternos axos' should read 'ternos axes', and 'Quodsi jam z fuerit punctum' should be the capital point label 'Z'.
